quartiers:The Old Town.name: The Old Town
quartiers:The Old Town.teaser: One limestone street, five squares and the side lanes where Dubrovnik still eats: time it against the ships
quartiers:The Old Town.story: Walk in at Pile and the Stradun pulls you straight to Ploče, its paving polished by centuries of shoes until it shines after rain and turns slick underfoot. The life is off to the sides. Luža square gathers the Sponza, St Blaise and the bell tower; Gundulić square has its morning stalls under the poet's statue; Poljana Boškovića sits at the foot of the Jesuit Stairs. Climb the narrow lanes, Antuninska, Boškovićeva, Palmotićeva, and the menus shrink to one language. Up on Prijeko the touts work the tables. In late October the cruise traffic is thinning, but on a two-ship day the town still fills from mid-morning.
quartiers:The Old Town.why: Come before nine or after half past six, and turn uphill off the Stradun for every meal.
facts: The Stradun, the squares of Luža, Gundulić and Poljana Boškovića, and the stepped side lanes

quartiers:Pile.name: Pile
quartiers:Pile.teaser: Every taxi, coach and bus ends at Pile: cross the drawbridge, or turn left for the fort on its rock
quartiers:Pile.story: Pile is the land door of the city and it still behaves like one: buses swinging round the stop, coach groups gathering under a guide's paddle, taxis idling by the moat garden. Above the outer gate the drawbridge chains still hang; St Blaise stands in his niche over the arch. Step through and Onofrio's great fountain is the first thing you meet. Outside, Brsalje runs to the terrace of Nautika in the old Nautical School, and a path drops to Kolorina cove and climbs to Lovrijenac on its rock. This is also where you catch the bus out to Gruž and Lapad.
quartiers:Pile.why: Sit on Brsalje at dusk, with Bokar on one side and Lovrijenac on the other, before you go in.
facts: Pile Gate and its drawbridge, Brsalje's sea terrace and the path to Lovrijenac

quartiers:Ploče.name: Ploče
quartiers:Ploče.teaser: Out through Ploče Gate: the old quarantine halls, a town beach and the best view back at the walls
quartiers:Ploče.story: Ploče is where the city faced east, towards the caravan roads and the plague that rode them. Cross the bridge from the Revelin and the road runs past the long stone halls of Lazareti, then drops to Banje beach with the walls and Lokrum in the same frame. Above the road the cable car's lower station sends cabins up Srđ. Further on, the grand hotels stand along Frana Supila looking back at the town, and up Hvarska locals queue at Pizzeria Tabasco. At night, with the walls lit gold across the water, this is the side to sit on.
quartiers:Ploče.why: Eat outside here on a summer night: you get the floodlit walls without the Stradun prices.

quartiers:Gruž.name: Gruž
quartiers:Gruž.teaser: Where the ferries, the cruise ships and the morning fish all come in: Dubrovnik's working front door by sea
quartiers:Gruž.story: Gruž is the Dubrovnik that works for a living. Ferries for the Elaphiti and the coast load at the long quay, cruise ships tie up at the terminal and dwarf the stone houses, and at half past six the boats bring the fish to the market on Obala Stjepana Radića. Note that the ACI marina is not here: it sits about five kilometres further up the Rijeka Dubrovačka, at Komolac, where the inlet narrows. From Gruž, buses 1A and 1B reach Pile in a quarter of an hour or so. Go early, buy, have a coffee by the water, and you are back before the Old Town wakes.
quartiers:Gruž.why: Be at the market before nine: by ten the fish is gone and the quay belongs to the cruise coaches.

quartiers:Lapad.name: Lapad
quartiers:Lapad.teaser: Pine woods, a family bay and a car-free strip: where Dubrovnik lives when the Old Town is full
quartiers:Lapad.story: Lapad is the peninsula of hotels and flats west of Gruž, and it is where the city goes to swim and stroll. The pedestrian Šetalište kralja Zvonimira runs down under its plane trees to the beach in Uvala Lapad, lined with cafés where grandparents and students share the benches. Behind it rises Petka, a pine and holm-oak forest park of about 192 metres, with paths up to views of the Elaphiti; Babin Kuk spreads its hotels at the far end. This is where Dubrovnik lives rather than visits, and the evening walk along the bay is its own reason to come.

curiosities:A ruler for one month.name: A ruler for one month
curiosities:A ruler for one month.teaser: The Republic of Ragusa feared one man more than any fleet, so it gave its head of state a month
curiosities:A ruler for one month.story: For four and a half centuries, from the Treaty of Zadar in 1358 to Marmont's decree of 1808, Ragusa ran itself on suspicion of ambition. Every noble entered the Major Council at eighteen; it chose a Senate of patricians over forty, the standard count is 45, for a year at a time; a seven-member Minor Council handled the day. On top sat a Rector who served exactly one month, had to wait two years before he could stand again, and lived shut inside his palace for the whole term, leaving it only on state business. Nobody was meant to get used to power.
curiosities:A ruler for one month.why: It explains the whole city: a merchant aristocracy that trusted no single man, and kept its independence that way.
facts: Stand in the atrium of the Rector's Palace (its own card is under Culture) and look up at the rooms he could not leave
The Senate's size and the Major Council's entry age changed over the centuries; 45 senators and about 300 nobles are the usual figures, not fixed ones

curiosities:The wind that excused a crim.name: The wind that excused a crime
curiosities:The wind that excused a crim.teaser: Dubrovnik swears its old Senate stopped work when the jugo blew: a lovely story with no paper behind it
curiosities:The wind that excused a crim.story: The jugo comes up from the south-east, warm and wet, piling the sea against the rocks below the walls and pressing on the head like a hand. Dubrovnik tells a story about it: that the Republic's councils would not sit or pass sentence while it blew, and that a crime done in a hard jugo earned a lighter penalty, because the wind was known to unsettle judgement. Travel writers repeat it as law. Look for the statute, though, and it is not there: the story lives in folklore collections and guidebooks, not in any archive anyone cites. People still blame the jugo for headaches and short tempers.
curiosities:The wind that excused a crim.why: Treat it as what Dubrovnik feels about its weather, not as Republic law.
facts: Walk out to the rocks at Pile or Ploče on a jugo day in autumn or winter and watch the swell break against the walls

curiosities:Why every façade matches.name: Why every façade matches
curiosities:Why every façade matches.teaser: The Stradun looks designed in one go because, after 1667, it was: a rebuild run by rule from Rome
curiosities:Why every façade matches.story: On the morning of 6 April 1667 the ground shook for a few seconds and the medieval city came down; fires burned for days after. The Rector was among the dead. The man who saved the shape of the place never saw it: Stjepan Gradić, a Ragusan priest who ran the Vatican Library, lobbied the Pope and Europe's courts for money and pressed the Senate to rebuild rather than move. What rose was Baroque and regulated: the Stradun's houses at one height, shops below with the door and the counter window under a single arch, flats above. That sameness is policy, not chance.
curiosities:Why every façade matches.why: Look at the ground floors: the door-and-counter arches repeat, house after house.
facts: Walk the Stradun and count the matching shop arches; the Sponza is one of the few buildings that came through the quake (its own card)
The death toll: Robin Harris counts about 2,000 inside the walls, older sources up to 5,000; the magnitude (about 7) is a modern estimate

curiosities:Marin Držić.name: Marin Držić
curiosities:Marin Držić.teaser: The Renaissance comic who mocked Dubrovnik's grandees, and later plotted to overthrow them
curiosities:Marin Držić.story: Marin Držić was born in the city in 1508, trained as a priest, and spent his life broke, restless and very funny. His Dundo Maroje, first staged in 1551, sends a miser to Rome after his spendthrift son and lets the servant Pomet run rings round everyone: Croatian theatre still starts there, and the Summer Festival keeps staging it. Late in life he wrote to the Medici in Florence asking for help to topple the patrician government that had laughed at his plays. Nothing came of it. He died in Venice in 1567. His house on Široka is now a small museum of his stage world.
curiosities:Marin Držić.why: See a Držić play in Croatian if one is on: you will follow Pomet without a word of the language.
facts: The House of Marin Držić, Široka 7; the capon dish at Kopun on Poljana Boškovića (its own card)

curiosities:Ruđer Bošković.name: Ruđer Bošković
curiosities:Ruđer Bošković.teaser: A Jesuit from these lanes guessed in 1758 that matter is points held apart by forces
curiosities:Ruđer Bošković.story: Ruđer Josip Bošković was born in the Old Town on 18 May 1711, joined the Jesuits in Rome, and became one of the great scientific minds of his century: astronomer, mathematician, surveyor, diplomat for his Republic. His Theoria Philosophiae Naturalis, printed in Vienna in 1758, pictured matter not as hard little balls but as points with forces between them, repulsive up close and attractive further off. Two centuries later physicists recognised atomic and field ideas in it, and Heisenberg is credited with calling him the Croatian Leibniz. He was a Fellow of the Royal Society in London and died in Milan in 1787.
curiosities:Ruđer Bošković.why: Stand at the foot of the Jesuit Stairs: the square there carries his name.
facts: Poljana Ruđera Boškovića at the foot of the Jesuit Stairs, the steps Game of Thrones used for Cersei's walk

culture:The Rector's Palace.name: The Rector's Palace
culture:The Rector's Palace.teaser: A palace twice blown up by its own gunpowder, rebuilt with a Renaissance portico and a sailor's bust
culture:The Rector's Palace.story: The Republic kept its gunpowder in the building where it kept its head of state, and paid for it twice. An explosion in 1435 wrecked the old fortified residence; Onofrio della Cava, the Neapolitan who built the city's fountains, raised a late-Gothic palace in its place. A second blast in 1463 tore it again, and Michelozzo of Florence and Juraj Dalmatinac worked on the repair, which is why Gothic windows sit over a Renaissance portico of carved capitals. Inside the arcaded atrium stands the bust of Miho Pracat, the ship-owner from Lopud, the one private citizen the Republic honoured that way. Upstairs, the Cultural History Museum fills the state rooms.
culture:The Rector's Palace.why: Linger in the atrium: in summer it is one of the Festival's concert halls, and its acoustics are why.
facts: Pred Dvorom, between Luža square and the cathedral, Old Town

culture:Sponza and the Memorial Room.name: Sponza and the Memorial Room
culture:Sponza and the Memorial Room.teaser: The Republic weighed its trade in this courtyard; today one room holds the faces of those who defended it
culture:Sponza and the Memorial Room.story: Paskoje Miličević built the Sponza between 1516 and 1522 as the Republic's customs house, with its mint and treasury; every bale landed at the port passed under its arch, where a Latin line warns that the weights do not allow cheating, for God weighs with the weigher. It came through the 1667 quake and now keeps the Dubrovnik State Archives. In one wing is the Memorial Room of the Defenders: photographs of the men killed in the siege of 1991-92, which began on 1 October 1991. On 6 December 1991 alone the shelling killed 19 people and wounded 60. Most visitors pass in under a minute. Stay longer.
culture:Sponza and the Memorial Room.why: Read a few names and ages in the Memorial Room: most of them were barely twenty.

culture:Lazareti.name: Lazareti
culture:Lazareti.teaser: Ten stone halls outside Ploče Gate where caravans and their cargo waited out the plague before entering
culture:Lazareti.story: In 1377 Ragusa's Major Council made travellers from infected places wait outside the city before they entered. The halls beyond Ploče Gate came much later, dated 1627 by the World Monuments Fund and to work between about 1590 and 1642 by other accounts: a line of stone warehouses with walled yards where traders off the Ottoman roads, their goods and their animals sat out their days under guard. Today the halls are a cultural centre. In summer the Linđo Folklore Ensemble dances here under the vaults, a dance-master on the lijerica calling the steps. The season ended in early October.

provisioning:Gundulić Square market.name: Gundulić Square market
provisioning:Gundulić Square market.teaser: A morning of stalls under the poet's statue: candied orange peel, dried figs and lavender
provisioning:Gundulić Square market.story: Under the bronze of the poet Ivan Gundulić, cast by Ivan Rendić and unveiled in May 1893, a handful of stalls set up each morning and are packing away by about midday. provisioning:The oyster quay at Mali Sto.teaser: Buy from the growers themselves at Mali Ston: bring ice and a cool box, and ring ahead out of season
provisioning:The oyster quay at Mali Sto.story: Taking oysters back to the galley is a matter of logistics. Bring a cool box, ice and cash in small notes. Through the busy months the growers' boats tie up at the Mali Ston waterfront and sell oysters and mussels straight from the bay. By late October the quay is quiet, so do not count on finding someone there. Telephone a grower or Bota Šare the day before and arrange a pick-up. Several farms, at Mali Ston, Zamaslina, Hodilje and Luka, also take visitors out to the beds by boat. Keep the oysters cold, cupped side down, and open them on board.

provisioning:Saints Hills.name: Saints Hills
provisioning:Saints Hills.teaser: An abandoned stone winery at Oskorušno, revived by the Tolj family, pours its reds on the roof
provisioning:Saints Hills.story: The cellar house at Oskorušno had been a working winery until its owners left for overseas. Of the two flagship Plavac Malis, Sveta Lucija comes from the Dingač slopes and Sveti Roko from Komarna, across the channel. There is an Istrian white too, the Malvazija called Nevina.

provisioning:The Franciscan pharmacy.name: The Franciscan pharmacy
provisioning:The Franciscan pharmacy.teaser: Friars have dispensed medicine inside Pile Gate since 1317: buy the rose cream, see the old jars
provisioning:The Franciscan pharmacy.story: The Friars Minor opened their pharmacy in 1317, and it has dispensed medicine ever since, now from a counter just inside Pile Gate. It was among the first in Europe to serve the general public, not only the monks. What a visitor takes away is the creams, made from local plants to the friars' old formulas: rose cream, almond oil, lavender and pine balms. Painted jars, mortars and ledgers from the early apothecary sit in the monastery museum off the Romanesque cloister.

walks:The city walls.name: The city walls
walks:The city walls.teaser: A one-way walk of 1,940 m round the rooftops, from the Pile bastions to Minčeta and back to the gate
walks:The city walls.story: Climb from Pile Gate past Bokar, Michelozzo's two-storey casemate of 1461-63, and follow the sea wall east above the rocks, the swell sounding below, terracotta roofs and washing lines. The ring turns north round the harbour and up to Minčeta, the round tower of 1464 by Michelozzo and Juraj Dalmatinac: at 25 m the highest point. Across the cove Lovrijenac sits on its own 37 m rock, its seaward walls 12 m thick, its city-facing ones 60 cm, so the city could bring it down if it were ever lost. Over its door: Non bene pro toto libertas venditur auro. Your ticket covers it; Hamlet plays there in summer.
walks:The city walls.why: From Minčeta you see the whole Stradun from above, the view that explains how the city is laid out.

walks:Stradun and the five squares.story: Start at Pile with Onofrio's great fountain of 1438. The water once came from a spring 12 km away, and it still pours from sixteen stone masks. Finish on Bunićeva poljana by the cathedral, a few steps from the Old Port.

walks:Mount Srđ and Fort Imperial.story: The cable car lifts you from above Buža Gate to the summit of Srđ, about 412 m above the sea, in a few minutes. On a still day you can hear the gulls from both. Coming down to Mali Ston you arrive at the oyster tables of Bota Šare.

walks:The Ljuta and its mills.story: Konavle was the Republic's grain field, and the Ljuta ground its flour. One mill still turns and grinds flour, and the source and the upper river are protected. Afterwards, lunch at Konoba Konavoski Dvori, by the water.

calas:Banje.teaser: The city's own pebble beach, two minutes outside Ploče Gate, with the walls rising behind your towel
calas:Banje.story: Banje is where Dubrovnik goes for a swim without leaving town. calas:The rocks under the south wall.story: There is no beach on the seaward side of the Old Town, only the rock the walls stand on. Go past the cathedral and through one of the small openings in the south wall by the Buža bars and you come out on flat shelves of pale limestone just above the water. Steel ladders lead down into the sea, which is deep and clear straight off the rock, and on summer afternoons the sound is of bodies hitting water as people jump from the higher ledges. calas:Lokrum.name: Lokrum
calas:Lokrum.teaser: A wooded reserve ten minutes off the Old Port, with peacocks, a salt lake and a rule: everyone leaves by night
calas:Lokrum.story: Lokrum sits about 600 m off the Old Port and nobody lives on it: overnight stays are banned, and the last boat takes everyone back to town in the evening. Benedictines founded an abbey here in 1023; Archduke Maximilian of Habsburg bought the island in the 1850s, built a summer house on the monastery ruins, laid out gardens and brought peacocks, whose descendants still strut the paths and scream from the pines. The island has been a protected reserve since 1964. Walk from the harbour to the cloister, where a replica Iron Throne recalls the Game of Thrones filming, then on to the Mrtvo More, the 'Dead Sea', a small salt lake fed by the sea through the rock, warm, sheltered and shallow enough for children. The southern shore is bare rock dropping into deep water.
calas:Lokrum.why: The quietest swim within sight of the walls, and a pine-shaded walk when the Old Town is full.

calas:Lopud and Šunj.name: Lopud and Šunj
calas:Lopud and Šunj.teaser: The ferry to Lopud, then a walk across the island through pines to the rare thing on this coast: sand
calas:Lopud and Šunj.story: Lopud is the middle of the three inhabited Elaphiti islands, the name from the Greek for deer, and the one with the beach. Step off the ferry onto the village waterfront and take the lane inland near the ruins of the old Grand Hotel; a signed path climbs through shady pine woods and drops to Šunj on the far side. It is a sandy bay protected by a breakwater, shallow for about 100 m, which on a coast of pebbles and rock is the reason people make the trip. Visitors leave cars behind: in summer golf carts shuttle between port and beach. In late October the sea is around 20 °C, the beach bars and rentals are winding down and the island goes quiet.

avoid:The cruise-day crush.name: The cruise-day crush
avoid:The cruise-day crush.teaser: On a big ship day, thousands of day visitors pour through Pile Gate within a few hours
avoid:The cruise-day crush.story: Dubrovnik's cruise berths are at Gruž, a few kilometres from the walls, and when the big ships are in, buses and shuttles deliver their passengers to Pile Gate in a single wave. Stradun, a street about 300 m long, then carries thousands of day visitors at once and the walls queue at the stairs. The city has pushed back: the Port Authority limits berthing to two large ships a day and has capped cruise visitors in town at about 4,000 at a time, yet some 461 cruise calls were scheduled for 2026. The ships keep to a timetable, so the crush can be planned around.

avoid:Prijeko Street.name: Prijeko Street
avoid:Prijeko Street.teaser: The long lane parallel to Stradun where the menus come in eight languages and a waiter blocks your way
avoid:Prijeko Street.story: Prijeko runs the length of the Old Town one block north of Stradun, a straight lane of terraces under the stairs that climb to the walls. It has become the town's tourist-menu row: laminated cards in eight to ten languages, photos of every dish, hosts stepping into your path, and 'fresh fish' that has often come from a freezer. The exception is Stara Loža, the one Prijeko address this guide keeps (its own card is under the tables). The honest konobas are a stair or two away, in the side lanes that cross between Stradun and the walls.

avoid:Oysters inside the walls.name: Oysters inside the walls
avoid:Oysters inside the walls.teaser: The oysters on Old Town menus come from Mali Ston, an hour up the coast: eat them there instead
avoid:Oysters inside the walls.story: Dubrovnik's oysters are not from Dubrovnik. They are farmed in the bay at Mali Ston, about an hour north-west by road, and reach the Old Town by van. An oyster keeps, but it does not improve: a plate inside the walls may have spent days in transit and cold storage, especially in the shoulder season when restaurants buy less often, and it is served at Old Town prices. At Mali Ston the same shellfish comes off the rafts in the bay you are looking at. The oyster itself, its protected name and its season, have their own card under the table.

avoid:Truffle on the menu.teaser: Croatia's truffle country is Istria, far to the north: here it is usually imported, or oil
avoid:Truffle on the menu.story: Truffle is the flavour of Istria, at the other end of the Croatian coast, where the oak woods of the Mirna valley are hunted with dogs. It is not part of the Dubrovnik kitchen, and when it turns up on an Old Town menu, shaved over pasta or in a 'truffle risotto', it has either travelled a long way or come out of a bottle of truffle-flavoured oil. A menu that leads with truffle is telling you it was written for visitors. The local plate is elsewhere: šporki makaruli, black risotto, brodet, the lamb from under the peka.

craft:Do this one.name: AR Atelier, Gruda
craft:Do this one.teaser: A painter in Konavle raises her own silkworms and teaches the stitch of the valley's costume
craft:Do this one.story: In a stone house at Gruda, at the far end of Konavle, the academic painter Antonia Rusković Radonić keeps silkworms on mulberry leaves from March to November, reels the thread and dyes it, then works it into the tight geometric Konavle embroidery that edges the women's costume worn at Easter. Croatia protects both the silk-making and the embroidery as national heritage. A weekly embroidery circle of local women has met here for more than fifteen years. Visitors are shown the costume collection, then handed cloth, needle and silk to try a pattern of their own. In late October the last silkworms of the season are still feeding.

drink:Plavac Mali.name: Plavac Mali
drink:Plavac Mali.teaser: The little blue grape of Pelješac, and a DNA hunt that found Zinfandel's family tree in Dalmatia
drink:Plavac Mali.story: Plavac Mali means little blue, and it is the red of every Dalmatian table. For years Californians, Mike Grgich among the believers, said it was Zinfandel. In 1998 Carole Meredith of UC Davis began testing with Ivan Pejić and Edi Maletić of the University of Zagreb and found it was not the same grape, but related. In December 2001 Pejić brought her a near-extinct vine from Kaštela called Crljenak Kaštelanski: it matched Zinfandel and Primitivo exactly. The team's 2004 paper showed Plavac Mali to be the child of that grape and Dobričić, a variety from the island of Šolta. So Zinfandel is Plavac's parent, not its twin.
drink:Plavac Mali.why: Order it with brodet or lamb from the peka: big, dark, dried-fig fruit and alcohol that often passes 14%.
facts: Deep ruby, dried cherry and fig, firm tannin, high alcohol

drink:Dingač.name: Dingač
drink:Dingač.teaser: Plavac Mali from 45° slopes above the sea, reached through a 400 m tunnel the growers paid for
drink:Dingač.story: Dingač is a strip of near-vertical vineyard between Trstenik and Podobuče on the south face of Pelješac, and in 1961 it became the first protected wine name in Yugoslavia. Growers say the grapes cook three times: from the sun, from the sea's glare and from the white stones. For centuries the harvest came out on donkeys along goat paths. Then the vineyard owners' cooperative borrowed the money and had a 400 m tunnel cut through the ridge from Potomje; it opened on 29 November 1975 and turned a 20 km detour into 4. Today you drive through it, single file, in the dark.
drink:Dingač.why: Drive the Potomje tunnel and come out above the open sea and the steepest vines in Croatia.
facts: Plavac Mali at full ripeness: dark, raisined, warm, often above 14%

drink:Pošip.name: Pošip
drink:Pošip.teaser: Korčula's white, from the linked fields of Smokvica and Čara, made for Mali Ston oysters
drink:Pošip.story: Pošip grows almost only on Korčula, in the Smokvica and Čara fields at the centre of the island. Local tradition credits Marin Tomašić of Čara with finding the vine in 1864, and in 1967 it became the first Croatian white given protected status. DNA puts its parents as Bratovina and Zlatarica blatska, two old island grapes. The wine is broad, low in acid, with citrus, almond and a saline finish, usually 13.5 to 14.5%. On this coast it is the bottle opened with oysters on the Mali Ston quay and the lunch white on every boat.
drink:Pošip.why: The white for shellfish: it has the weight to stand next to a flat oyster without disappearing.
facts: Straw gold, citrus peel, almond, salt; soft acidity, 13.5–14.5%

drink:Grk.name: Grk
drink:Grk.teaser: A white that grows only in Lumbarda's sand, from a vine that cannot pollinate itself
drink:Grk.story: Grk means the Greek, and it grows only around Lumbarda, at the eastern tip of Korčula, in sandy soil between the stone walls. Greek settlers from Issa, today's Vis, did found a colony here in the 3rd or 4th century BC, but nobody can prove they brought this vine. The botany is proven: Grk has functionally female flowers, so growers plant Plavac Mali between the rows to pollinate it. Even then the bunches set unevenly and yields are tiny. Fewer than ten estates bottle it. The wine is dry, bitter-almond, saline and herbal.
drink:Grk.why: Taste a vine that needs a red grape beside it to bear fruit at all.
facts: Dry, pale gold, bitter almond, sage, salt

drink:Prošek.name: Prošek
drink:Prošek.teaser: Dalmatia's raisin-grape dessert wine, and a fight over its name that Brussels has still not settled
drink:Prošek.story: Prošek is made from grapes left to shrivel, on the vine or on mats in the sun, until the sugar is so dense that the wine stays sweet: amber, raisin, fig and walnut, closer to an old sweet wine than to anything sparkling. When Croatia joined the EU in 2013 it had to drop the name on its labels because Italy said it sounded like Prosecco. Croatia applied again; the Commission published the request in 2021 and received objections from Italy and others. The new EU geographical-indications regulation of 2024 set rules for similar names, but we found no final decision on Prošek as of October 2026.

drink:Travarica and the home rakija.teaser: Herb, grape, green walnut and rose petal: the four bottles a Dubrovnik house keeps
drink:Travarica and the home rakija.story: Before a meal in a Konavle house someone pours travarica: clear grape rakija with sage, rosemary, fennel and immortelle steeped in it, sharp and green. Loza is the plain grape spirit of the coast. Orahovac starts with walnuts picked unripe around St John's Day, 24 June, left forty days or more in rakija with cloves, cinnamon and sugar until it turns dark amber. Rozalin, or rozulin, is the Dubrovnik one: a rose-petal liqueur, made at home, that perfumes the city's rožata custard. Most of the best is never sold; it comes out of an unlabelled bottle.

bars:Buža.story: Buža is Dubrovnik dialect for hole, and that is the entrance: a gap in the southern sea wall below the cathedral quarter, signed for cold drinks and the view. listening:Linđo at Lazareti.name: Linđo at Lazareti
listening:Linđo at Lazareti.teaser: One bowed lyre, a stamping foot and a ring of Konavle dancers under the old quarantine vaults
listening:Linđo at Lazareti.story: The lijerica is a small pear-shaped fiddle with three strings, held upright on the knee and bowed. Its player sits in the middle of the floor and beats time with his foot on the stone while a caller shouts the figures in rhyme, and the dancers around him turn, swap partners, speed up and stop on command. That is the Linđo, the dance of the Konavle valley and the Dubrovnik coast. The Linđo Folklore Ensemble, founded in the mid-1960s, keeps it alive and stages it on summer nights in the Lazareti, the long row of stone halls just past the Ploče Gate, in full Konavle costume.

listening:Klapa in the churches.story: Klapa is Dalmatian multipart singing without instruments, a small group of mostly male voices in a close half-ring, the first tenor leading; UNESCO inscribed it in 2012. listening:Oliver Dragojević.name: Oliver Dragojević
listening:Oliver Dragojević.teaser: The singer a whole coast followed to sea: Split to Vela Luka by boat, July 2018
listening:Oliver Dragojević.story: Oliver Dragojević was born in Split in December 1947 and grew up in Vela Luka on Korčula, and for half a century his husky, unhurried voice was the sound of the Dalmatian coast: klapa harmony underneath, a jazz shadow on top. listening:Gibonni.name: Gibonni
listening:Gibonni.teaser: The Split songwriter who wrote Cesarica, then gave many of his Porin statuettes away
listening:Gibonni.story: Zlatan Stipišić, Gibonni, was born in Split in August 1968 and sings in the Dalmatian dialect over rock and pop arrangements that never lose the klapa line underneath. He has won Croatia's Porin music award more often than almost anyone, five in a single night when Tolerancija was album of the year. around:Cavtat.name: Cavtat
around:Cavtat.teaser: A pine-dark peninsula, a painter's birthplace and a white marble tomb at the very top
around:Cavtat.story: Cavtat sits on a double bay south of the airport, the old Epidaurum whose refugees are said to have founded Dubrovnik. Walk the palm-lined harbour to Bukovčeva street and the house where Vlaho Bukovac, the painter, was born in 1855; his studio and early pictures are inside. Then climb through the pines of the Rat peninsula to the cemetery at the top, where Ivan Meštrović built the Račić family mausoleum in 1920-22, a domed chapel of pale Brač stone with carved angels and a bronze bell, for a shipowning family that lost its son to the Spanish flu. The view runs back across the bay to the city.

around:Sokol Grad.name: Sokol Grad
around:Sokol Grad.teaser: The Republic's falcon fort, grown out of a limestone crag at the Konavle frontier
around:Sokol Grad.story: Sokol grows out of a rock above Dunave, high in Konavle; it is hard to see where cliff ends and masonry begins. Bronze Age, Roman and Byzantine finds show the rock was held long before Ragusa. It is named in 1373, passed to the Republic with the Sanković donation of Konavle in 1391, and from about 1420 the Ragusans rebuilt and armed it as their watch on the inland border. Why it emptied is argued: the 1667 earthquake, 1672, or the Cretan War. The Society of Friends of Dubrovnik Antiquities took on the ruin in 1970 and opened it to visitors in 2013.

around:Trsteno Arboretum.name: Trsteno Arboretum
around:Trsteno Arboretum.teaser: A Ragusan noble's summer garden from the 1490s, survivor of shells and a wildfire, above a tiny harbour
around:Trsteno Arboretum.story: Ivan Marinov Gučetić began the summer villa and garden at Trsteno in 1494, and his family, the Gozze, kept adding to it for four centuries: Renaissance beds, a pergola walk, a baroque grotto and Neptune fountain. Ragusan captains brought seeds home. In 1948 Vito Gozze gave the estate to the Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts. In early October 1991 shelling from the sea set much of it alight, and in the drought summer of 2000 a forest fire burned some 120,000 square metres. Two giant oriental planes in the village square, said to be over 500 years old, survived both.

On a small island in the larger lake stands St Mary's, a Benedictine monastery and church first built in the 12th century; a park boat takes you across.
